How do we choose the next LDL-C lowering therapy for a patient with established ASCVD? This is a question we face often in preventive cardiology, and one that deserves better comparative evidence. Pleased to share this American Journal of Preventive Cardiology study by Nihar Desai Yale School of Medicine and colleagues, together with the accompanying editorial by Safi U. Khan MD, MS. and Raul Santos I would encourage reading the two together https://lnkd.in/gK6eYEf3 https://lnkd.in/gwtcVmYp In their target trial emulation, evolocumab initiation was associated with a 20% lower hazard of fatal or nonfatal MI (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.70–0.91). Among the 41.4% with baseline LDL-C available, weighted four-year MI risk estimates were 5.88% versus 7.76%, an absolute difference of 1.88 percentage points. Results were similar when changes in background statin use were allowed (HR 0.79). The authors deserve credit for addressing a practical clinical question with careful attention to study design and prespecified checks for potential bias. Editorialists provide a thoughtful perpsective -Treatment choice in routine care reflects statin intolerance, prior response, insurance approval, affordability, and patient preference. -Claims data capture these factors incompletely. -A prescription filled doesnt equate medication was consistently taken -Pts on one treatment vs other can be very different -Baseline LDL-C missing in 58.6%,. -4 year estimates therefore depend substantially on modeling assumptions. These limitations leave uncertainty about how much of the observed difference is caused by treatment. Next steps? A useful pragmatic considered would be a direct randomized comparison of treatment strategies, such as early evolocumab versus ezetimibe-first escalation, with appropriate background therapy and further intensification when needed. Serial coronary imaging could examine changes in plaque burden and composition alongside achieved LDL-C and treatment persistence. How can it influence our practice? For me, the practical message is to start with the patient’s LDL-C gap, underlying risk, and ability to sustain treatment. Ezetimibe remains an appropriate option when it can achieve the required reduction. Patients who need substantially greater lowering deserve timely consideration of more potent therapy. Getting to goal and staying there should guide that discussion. In Nature Medicine today, ahead of Sudheesha Perera 's #AHA26 presentation, our study maps cardiovascular need and digital readiness across nearly 83,000 US census tracts. We asked an important policy question: Where can digital cardiovascular care expand access, and where do we first need to invest to make it possible? Among high-burden communities with cardiology workforce constraints: • 19.9 million residents live in higher-readiness communities, where digital care could be deployed now. • 74.1 million live in lower-readiness communities, where connectivity, devices, affordability and adoption support are needed alongside clinical deployment. Nearly two-thirds of the lower-readiness group lived in metropolitan counties, and neighboring tracts in the same county often had different priorities. Our public dashboard lets clinicians, health systems and policymakers search their county and explore priorities neighborhood by neighborhood. Patients with stable chest symptoms and suspected CAD were approximately twice as likely to experience a more favorable outcome with coronary plaque-based care than with usual care. That is the top-line result of the randomized PARAMOUNT trial, which I presented today at #AHA26 . The trial and this post were sponsored by @Cleerly; I am PARAMOUNT co-chair and a paid consultant to Cleerly. What was compared 523 patients with stable, symptomatic suspected CAD and LDL-C >100 mg/dL were analyzed after 1:1 randomization at 21 U.S. sites: • Coronary plaque-based care: CCTA with AI-based quantitative plaque and ischemia analysis (AI-QCT). Plaque stage set the LDL-C goal and guided medical therapy and revascularization decisions. • Usual care: functional stress testing, then guideline-based care per the treating physician. How the primary endpoint worked A hierarchical win ratio compared every plaque-based care patient with every usual-care patient on four outcomes, ranked by clinical priority: 1. Diagnostic certainty of angina attributed to CAD 2. Greater LDL-C reduction at 180 days 3. Freedom from ICA without obstructive CAD 4. Freedom from PCI without significant stenosis The win ratio is the number of comparisons won divided by the number lost. 1.0 means no advantage; 2.0 means twice as many wins as losses. The results • Win ratio 2.0 (95% CI 1.37–2.56; P < 0.0001) • Driven mainly by improved diagnostic certainty (net 16.64% of patient pairs) and LDL-C reduction (net 6.36%) • LDL-C fell 15.1% with plaque-based care vs. 8.5% with usual care at 180 days (P = 0.023) My take as a cardiac imager What stands out to me is where the benefit came from: the largest share came from diagnostic certainty. Quantifying the plaque itself, rather than relying on a functional test alone, gave clinicians and patients a clearer answer about whether symptoms were due to CAD, and plaque stage then set how aggressively LDL-C was treated. Swipe through the slides for the full summary. Trial registration: NCT06713239 #PARAMOUNT #CardiacImaging #CCTA #Cardiology

A new model of decentralized cardiovascular research is taking shape Pts can be identified through clinical records, contacted directly, and enrolled remotely, testing arranged at local labs-->brings selected research activities closer to where people live Participation more manageable around work, travel and family responsibilities (more practical) In American Journal of Preventive Cardiology sim pub with American Heart Association #AHA26 presentation Mitsuaki Sawano Harlan Krumholz Yuan Lu put this approach into practice through UNRAVEL, studying Lp(a) in adults with ASCVD across the nation https://lnkd.in/g-QBhG5d >20K individuals contacted, of >2K prescreening respondents, 922 enrolled participants in record time (13 months), lab completion rate 99.5%, 82% rated their overall experience as 9-10 out of 10. Amazing #'s. We dont see these in conventional research designs! In my accompanying editorial, “Knocking on New Doors: UNRAVELing the Future of Decentralized Cardiovascular Research” https://lnkd.in/gy88SJeT I discuss what it will take for this model to fulfill its promise 1. 90% of participants came from Connecticut. Making enrollment available remotely does not ensure that we reach different communities will require local clinicians, community organizations and people whom potential participants trust. 2. decentralized testing needs a clear connection back to care. Need to build direct connections to clinicians and measure what happens after testing. Participants should not have to carry that coordination alone. 3. Future studies should account cost considerations vs conventional approaches. 4. Next phase should bring multiple health systems together around common eligibility, coordinated oversight and shared outcomes. Each would recruit through its own clinical and community relationships. This could combine consistent scientific methods with wider local participation. Take home message? Biggest opportunity is to build research that fits more naturally into people’s lives, reaches a broader population, and connects discovery with care. Congratulations to Yale School of Medicine entire team for giving us a credible starting point. A new future of clinical studies is knocking at our door. We need to ensure that we are not simply knocking on the same doors American Society for Preventive Cardiology (ASPC)

Does measuring Lp(a) really change cardiovascular prevention? Lp(a) is a well-established cardiovascular risk factor, but identifying risk does not necessarily mean improving clinical outcomes. The Lp(a)HORIZON results reignite the debate: despite substantial Lp(a) reduction with pelacarsen, the trial did not meet its primary cardiovascular endpoint. This does not undermine the causal role of Lp(a), but raises an important question: when does measuring Lp(a) actually change clinical decisions and improve patient outcomes? A key challenge for the future of cardiovascular prevention. #LpA #Cardiology #Lipidology #CardiovascularPrevention https://lnkd.in/dTybBwWg
